subject: English
description: Common phrasal verbs (give up, look after, put off, run into, etc.) with meanings

questions.stem: The phrasal verb 'GIVE UP' most closely means:

options.option_text: To donate something to charity
To quit, abandon, or stop trying
To raise someone's hopes high
To return something borrowed

questions.explanation: GIVE UP — quit, surrender, stop trying. 'He gave up smoking last year'. Distractor 1 = GIVE AWAY (donate freely). Distractor 3 = BUILD UP (raise hopes). Distractor 4 = GIVE BACK (return).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The phrasal verb 'LOOK AFTER' most closely means:

options.option_text: To search for something lost
To take care of or be responsible for
To follow closely with the eyes
To resemble in appearance or manner

questions.explanation: LOOK AFTER — take care of. 'She looks after her elderly parents'. Distractor 1 = LOOK FOR. Distractor 3 = LOOK AT. Distractor 4 = TAKE AFTER ('She takes after her mother').
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The phrasal verb 'PUT OFF' most closely means:

options.option_text: To wear something on the body
To postpone, delay, or defer
To put something away in storage
To remove an item of clothing

questions.explanation: PUT OFF — postpone. 'The meeting was put off till next week.' Distractor 1 = PUT ON (wear). Distractor 3 = PUT AWAY (store). Distractor 4 = TAKE OFF (remove clothes). 'PUT OFF' can also mean discourage someone ('The smell put me off').
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The phrasal verb 'RUN INTO' most closely means:

options.option_text: To go very fast in athletics
To meet by chance unexpectedly
To pour liquid into a vessel
To exit a building hurriedly

questions.explanation: RUN INTO — meet by chance. 'I ran into an old friend at the airport.' Also 'encounter unexpectedly' for problems: 'We ran into trouble.' Distractor 1 = RUN FAST. Distractor 3 = POUR INTO. Distractor 4 = RUN OUT (of something).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The phrasal verb 'BREAK DOWN' (machine sense) most closely means:

options.option_text: To divide into smaller pieces
To stop working due to a fault
To enter forcefully without permission
To start running away from danger

questions.explanation: BREAK DOWN (of a machine, vehicle) — stop functioning. 'My car broke down on the highway.' Of a person — emotional collapse: 'She broke down in tears.' Distractor 1 = BREAK UP (split). Distractor 3 = BREAK IN (forced entry). Distractor 4 = BREAK AWAY (escape).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The phrasal verb 'CALL OFF' most closely means:

options.option_text: To telephone someone in another city
To cancel a planned event or activity
To shout instructions from a distance
To remove something from the wall

questions.explanation: CALL OFF — cancel. 'The match was called off due to rain.' Distractor 1 = MAKE A CALL. Distractor 3 = CALL OUT (shout). Distractor 4 = unrelated.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The phrasal verb 'FIGURE OUT' most closely means:

options.option_text: To make a list of all options
To understand or solve by thinking
To draw a chart on the board
To count the number in a group

questions.explanation: FIGURE OUT — understand, solve, work out. 'I can't figure out how this works.' Distractor 1 = LIST OUT. Distractor 3 = DRAW. Distractor 4 = COUNT. Other phrasal verbs of meaning 'understand': make out, work out, fathom out.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: In the sentence 'The young manager will TAKE OVER the department next month,' which meaning best fits TAKE OVER?

options.option_text: to begin a long journey toward professional success
to assume control or full responsibility of something
to hand over duties to a senior colleague promptly
to overlook the routine errors made by subordinates

questions.explanation: TAKE OVER means to assume control or responsibility, as the manager is succeeding to the role. Option C is the key distractor — 'hand over' is the opposite of 'take over'; it involves transferring, not receiving, control. Students sometimes confuse these two because both describe a transition of duties.

questions.stem: While sorting old files, the auditor CAME ACROSS several unsigned contracts. Which meaning best fits CAME ACROSS here?

options.option_text: to deliberately arrange a formal review of records
to discover something unexpectedly during a search
to reject documents that lack proper authorisation
to cross-reference files with an official database entry

questions.explanation: CAME ACROSS means to encounter or discover something by chance. The phrase 'while sorting' signals accidental discovery, not a deliberate hunt. Option A is wrong because it implies prior intent, which contradicts the incidental nature of the find entirely.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'The prolonged drought has BROUGHT ABOUT a severe food shortage,' which option is the closest replacement for BROUGHT ABOUT?

options.option_text: brought forward — rescheduled to an earlier date
brought out — published or revealed to the public
caused or produced as a direct natural consequence
brought in — introduced from an outside source or body

questions.explanation: BRING ABOUT means to cause something to happen. Option C paraphrases this precisely with 'caused or produced.' The distractors are all valid phrasal verbs in other contexts — brought forward (reschedule), brought out (publish), brought in (introduce) — but none carries the direct causal meaning needed here.

questions.stem: The management decided to HOLD OFF the product launch until customer feedback improved. What does HOLD OFF mean in this context?

options.option_text: to cancel the launch permanently due to unfavourable data
to delay or postpone until conditions become more favourable
to fast-track the release well ahead of the original schedule
to distribute the launch responsibilities across separate teams

questions.explanation: HOLD OFF means to temporarily delay an action while waiting for better conditions. It does not mean permanent cancellation. Option A is the prime distractor — candidates confuse 'hold off' with 'call off,' but the clause 'until feedback improved' confirms the delay is conditional, not final.

questions.stem: After missing several deadlines, Ramesh worked through the weekend to MAKE UP FOR lost time. Which meaning best fits MAKE UP FOR?

options.option_text: to fabricate a convincing excuse for every missed deadline
to compensate or recover a shortfall through additional effort
to calculate precisely the total number of hours wasted
to negotiate an official extension from the project manager

questions.explanation: MAKE UP FOR means to compensate for something lost or missed. Extra work is the means of compensation here. Option A exploits the confusion between 'make up' (fabricate, used alone) and 'make up for' (compensate, used with 'for'). The full prepositional phrase changes the meaning entirely.

questions.stem: Choose the sentence in which the underlined phrasal verb is used INCORRECTLY.

options.option_text: The finance minister SET ASIDE ₹500 crore for rural infrastructure.
The expedition team SET OUT early to reach base camp before nightfall.
The new automobile factory will SET OFF hundreds of jobs in the region.
The volunteers SET UP a help desk for the flood-affected families.

questions.explanation: SET OFF means to trigger, ignite, or begin a journey — it does NOT mean to create or generate jobs. The correct phrase for C would be SET UP (establish) or simply 'create.' Options A (reserve funds), B (begin a purposeful journey), and D (establish a facility) all use their respective phrasal verbs correctly.

questions.stem: Read: 'The party tried to PLAY DOWN the scam, but the evidence was hard to GLOSS OVER. The minister eventually managed to LIVE DOWN the scandal and RIDE OUT the electoral storm.' Which verb means 'to endure a difficult period and emerge without serious damage'?

options.option_text: PLAY DOWN — to minimise or downplay something's significance
GLOSS OVER — to conceal or skim past an issue superficially
LIVE DOWN — to recover one's reputation after public embarrassment
RIDE OUT — to endure a crisis until it passes without being overcome

questions.explanation: RIDE OUT (from the nautical image of a ship weathering a storm intact) means to survive a difficult situation without being destroyed by it. LIVE DOWN is the strongest distractor: it means regaining respectability after a disgrace over time, not surviving an ongoing crisis. All four phrasal verbs are tested simultaneously, demanding precise discrimination between closely related meanings.
